Monday. Zeenat opened the plan for the app update and deleted the cushions from each task. "Honest numbers only," she told the team. At the bottom she added one bar labelled Buffer, six days, just before the client date. Tarun frowned. "What if my task runs over?" "Then tell me, and we look together," said Zeenat.

Thursday, week three. Tarun's login task took two days longer than planned because the test server crashed. He said so at stand-up. The team took two days from the buffer, and every other task kept its date.

Friday, week five. The update went out with four days of buffer left. Zeenat wrote in the notes: buffer used once, for a real delay.

qa.q: How many days of buffer were left when the update went out?
qa.a: Four days of buffer were left when the update went out.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling on Monday when he asked what if his task runs over?
qa.a: Tarun felt uneasy about being caught short or blamed for an overrun, now that the padding was gone.

qa.q: What could the team do if the buffer were used up early?
qa.a: They could talk to the client about scope or dates as soon as possible and drop the least important item, instead of hiding the delay.

qa.q: How might the client see the update going out with buffer left?
qa.a: The client might see the team as reliable, having received the update before the agreed date.

grounding: Shows a team removing padding from tasks and holding one shared buffer before the deadline, used only for a real delay.

subtype: Approach: keeps one shared buffer at the end of the project [Revision]
passage:
Uday, you're adding two extra days to every task on that project plan. Let your Elizabeth Aunty tell you what we learned at the printing press, long before your time.
Everyone on my team padded their tasks. Typesetting, three extra days. Proofreading, two. Binding, four. The plan looked safe. But every task used all its padding, and we were still late.
One year our manager sat us down. She said, "Take the padding out of each task. Give me honest times. Then we'll keep one buffer, ten days, at the very end, before the delivery date. Nobody touches it unless something real goes wrong."
At first we were nervous. Then the big binding machine broke for six days. We took six from the buffer and still delivered on time, with four days left over.
That buffer belonged to everyone, so nobody wasted it.

qa.q: How long was the shared buffer at the end?
qa.a: Ten days, at the very end, before the delivery date.

qa.q: How did the team feel when the manager removed the padding?
qa.a: They felt nervous at first, since their safe-looking cushions were gone.

qa.q: When the binding machine broke, what choice did the team make, and why did it work?
qa.a: They took six days from the shared buffer, which covered a real delay and still left four days, so they delivered on time.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen the delivery that year?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and proven right, since the single buffer absorbed a real problem and nobody wasted it.

grounding: It shows a team removing padding from each task and holding one buffer before the deadline, using it only when a real delay happens.

subtype: Approach: keeps one shared buffer at the end of the project [Revision]
passage:
The school renovation had to be finished before the monsoon, and Pema, the site coordinator, had only nine weeks. Every contractor's estimate came padded: painters wanted three extra days, electricians four, the plumber a week.
Her deputy Rashmi added them up. "With all the padding, we finish two weeks after the rains start."
Pema took a red pen. "Everyone gives me their honest time. No cushions." Then she drew a block at the end of the chart. "Eight days here. Shared. Anyone who hits a real delay asks me, and we take from this."
The painters grumbled. But without their extra days, they started on the Monday instead of drifting in on Wednesday.
In week six, the cement delivery was stuck at a flooded bridge for three days. Pema took three days from the buffer.
The work finished with five buffer days unused, a week before the first heavy rain.

qa.q: How many buffer days were left unused at the end?
qa.a: The work finished with five buffer days unused.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt when the padded total came out two weeks late?
qa.a: Rashmi was probably worried, since that meant finishing after the rains started.

qa.q: Why was a shared buffer better than each contractor's padding?
qa.a: Because padding gets used up by each team, while a shared buffer is kept for real delays like the flooded bridge.

qa.q: How might the painters see Pema's new rule?
qa.a: They grumbled at losing their extra days, but it pushed them to start on time.

grounding: It shows a coordinator removing padding from each task and keeping one shared buffer before the deadline, used only when a real delay occurs.
